# Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 15 (Bi-Vb Pc15)
**ID:** Bi-Vb Pc15
**Section:** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga (bi-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 15
**Title (English, from literature):** Departing without taking leave
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-bi-vb-pc15
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul7.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 15 (Anāpucchāpakkamana, "Departing without taking leave") governs the conduct of nuns when visiting lay households, establishing an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for a nun who sits down in a house and then departs without informing or taking leave of the resident owner [SuttaCentral; Hüsken 1997]. According to the origin story (Vin IV 271–272), a nun who was a regular guest receiving daily meals from a certain family (*kulūpikā niccabhattikā*) sat on a seat (*āsana*, a type of sitting cushion) and departed unannounced [Hüsken 1997]. When the cushion could not be found, suspicion fell on the nun, though the lay family later recovered it upon searching the home, as highlighted in the commentary *Samantapāsādikā* [Hüsken 1997]. The rule was enacted to prevent monastic visitors from incurring suspicion of theft and to discourage over-familiarity that neglects ordinary etiquette expected of a guest [Hüsken 1997]. The word commentary specifies that crossing beyond the covered or designated space with the first foot incurs a *dukkaṭa*, and with the second foot, a *pācittiya* [Hüsken 1997].
The rule is closely connected in phrasing and subject matter with the subsequent rules Pācittiya 16 and 17 [Hüsken 1997]. Direct parallels are preserved in the Pali *Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha* (Pc 15) and *Parivāra*, as well as in the vinayas of other early Buddhist schools, including the Dharmaguptaka (Pc 83), Mahīśāsaka (Pc 165), Sarvāstivāda (Pc 143), and Mūlasarvāstivāda traditions preserved in Chinese and Tibetan (xct-mu-bi-vb-pc135) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches this distribution, recording cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Bhikṣuṇīvinaya* and the Tibetan *Bhikṣuṇīvinayavibhaṅga*, alongside extensive Pali-internal text reuse with Pācittiya 16 (longest match §1.12–2.3.8), Saṅghādisesa 3, and Pācittiya 17 [DharmaNexus]. An English translation has been prepared by Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
